strengths: Addresses important practical problem: KV cache compression's impact on multi-instruction prompting is insufficiently studied despite widespread deployment
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 compression methods × 2 models, 541 IFEval prompts, supplementary LongBench experiments, multiple metrics (accuracy, rank correlation, ROUGE-L, LLM-as-judge)
Clear problem characterization: Six well-articulated pitfalls with systematic analysis. Rank correlation elegantly isolates eviction bias from instruction difficulty
Excellent concrete case study: System prompt leakage demonstrates security implications and provides grounded evaluation framework
Strong reproducibility: Detailed appendices, algorithms, implementation details, extensive supplementary experiments support verification and reproduction
Practical solutions: Simple, implementable methods (whitelisting, fair eviction) show consistent improvements across compression methods
weaknesses: Limited scope constrains generalizability: Only 2 models (8B-14B, no larger scales or other families), only 5 compression methods (not recent ones like PyramidKV), explicitly offline-only focus

Critical applicability limitation: Focus on offline compression; paper argues but does not validate that issues arise in online compression, which dominates real deployments. Solutions incompatible with online settings

Solution limitations: Whitelisting requires manual keyword selection (not fully automated), ~2x compression overhead (Fig. 23K); Fair eviction assumes equal importance and well-formed instruction boundaries—often violated. Absolute improvements modest (0.01-0.20 in Table 1)

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Appendix J provides post-hoc hypotheses; lacks theoretical insight into why different methods exhibit orthogonal biases (e.g., K-Norm inversion). Leakage curve inversion at high compression unexplained

Evaluation concerns: Leakage testing uses only direct queries, not sophisticated adversarial attacks; only one benchmark (modified IFEval); ROUGE-L limitations underexplored (LLM-as-judge discrepancies relegated to appendix); no statistical significance testing
Presentation issues: Figure 2a dense and hard to parse; key results in appendices (LLM-as-judge, debiasing); 'fair eviction' definition could be introduced more clearly upfront

Limited methodological novelty: Non-uniform degradation is somewhat expected; whitelisting and proportional allocation are straightforward mitigations. Contribution is primarily empirical characterization
Missing guidance for practitioners: No analysis of when to use which solution; trade-off spaces underexplored; per-layer biases (Figure 27) interesting but underdeveloped

strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem addressing a genuine gap between standard benchmarks and realistic multi-instruction scenarios
Comprehensive and rigorous empirical investigation across 2 models and 5 compression methods with 541 test prompts and supplementary LongBench experiments
Systematic characterization of 6 pitfalls with complementary analyses (rank correlation, keep rate analysis, mechanistic hypotheses)
Novel security angle with system prompt leakage as compelling case study demonstrating real-world vulnerability
Practical solutions with demonstrated consistent improvements (Table 1); fair eviction is elegantly simple yet effective
Excellent presentation quality with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 7), clear narrative flow, and comprehensive reproducibility-focused appendices
Thoughtful supplementary analyses including runtime overhead (Appendix K), Pareto frontier analysis (Appendices G-H), and LLM-as-a-judge validation
weaknesses: Limited model and method coverage (2 models, 5 methods) constrains generalizability; no evaluation on recent models or novel compression approaches

Focus on offline compression only; solutions assume known prompt structure and decomposable instructions, limiting applicability to practical online/streaming scenarios where long-context compression matters most
Proposed solutions remain partially manual: whitelisting requires keyword identification, fair eviction requires prompt decomposition; automation relegated to future work without demonstration

Limited methodological novelty—whitelisting and fair eviction are incremental rather than transformative; contribution is primarily problem identification rather than fundamental advances in compression design

System prompt leakage evaluation has gaps: simple defense prompts, ROUGE-L may not capture all leakage types, LLM-as-a-judge only validated on Llama3, LongBench 3000-4000 word experiments fail due to weak baseline defense
Mechanistic analysis is speculative and incomplete (Appendix J): hypotheses about attention patterns lack empirical support through visualization or embedding analysis; K-Norm behavior unexplained
Statistical rigor concerns: most figures lack error bars/confidence intervals; improvements in Table 1 are sometimes small relative to reported noise; no significance testing
Fair eviction makes strong assumption that equal retention rates are optimal, though some instructions may deserve differential importance; λ-debiasing partially addresses but requires tuning
Experimental design uses modified IFEval (new dataset) rather than original; synthetic defense+directive setup may not reflect real system prompt complexity
No evaluation on naturally multi-instruction datasets or comparison with longer context alternatives (e.g., different attention mechanisms)

strengths: Identifies and empirically documents a real and practically important gap in KV cache compression research: existing work focuses on single-instruction benchmarks while real deployments involve multi-instruction scenarios (system prompts + queries)

Thorough empirical evaluation across 5 eviction policies and 2 models with well-designed experiments; Spearman correlation analysis (Figure 3) provides quantitative evidence of degradation heterogeneity
Compelling system prompt leakage case study effectively demonstrates security implications of non-uniform instruction degradation
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1 and degradation curves) that clearly convey findings
Proposes practical solutions (whitelisting and fair eviction) that are simple to implement and shown to be effective; detailed algorithms and implementation specifications provided
Good reproducibility: defense prompts, whitelisted tokens, detailed algorithm specifications, and reference to KVPress library included
weaknesses: Proposed solutions are incremental: whitelisting requires manual curation (not scalable), while fair eviction is straightforward proportional budget allocation. Solutions are pragmatic but lack intellectual novelty

Fair eviction requires knowing instruction boundaries in advance—a significant practical limitation that is underemphasized. No discussion of automatic boundary detection, limiting real-world applicability

Narrow evaluation scope: only 2 models tested (both relatively small); modified IFEval used without detailed specification; system prompt leakage is a specialized case study; unclear generalization to other tasks or much longer contexts

Mechanistic understanding is shallow: paper documents 'what' fails but not deeply 'why'. Root causes of eviction bias (especially for position-based methods) not explained; two facets of degradation identified but not formalized

Methodological concerns: no error bars/significance tests; ROUGE-L is simplistic for measuring leakage; defense strings are artificially simple; only greedy decoding tested; implications of rounding in Algorithm 1 not discussed
Fair eviction shows modest and inconsistent improvements across methods (Figure 10)—K-norm barely improves; no computational cost analysis; generalization to >2 instruction spans unclear

Missing comparative analysis: no evaluation of alternative mitigation strategies (selective compression, training-time adaptations); no discussion of trade-offs between improvements and computational overhead

Limited theoretical grounding: primarily empirical work lacking information-theoretic or mechanistic analysis of why multi-instruction compression is fundamentally harder; connection to attention mechanisms underexplored
Presentation issues: Figures 4-7 small and difficult to read; six 'pitfalls' somewhat redundant and overlapping; compression ratio definition could be clearer
